summary: In the Decapolis, Jesus feeds four thousand men, besides women and children, who have stayed with Him three days, using seven loaves and a few small fish.
key_insight: Here Jesus Himself raises the need, before the disciples say a word, and He gives His reason: “I have compassion on the multitude.” He has even thought about their walk home, “for some of them have come from afar.”
story: In those days Jesus was still on the eastern side of the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the Decapolis, and once again a very great crowd had gathered around Him. {Mk} They had stayed with Him for three days, and whatever food they had brought was gone.

Jesus called His disciples and said, “I have compassion on the multitude, because they have now continued with Me three days and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away hungry to their own houses, they will faint on the way; for some of them have come from afar.” {Mk}

His disciples answered, “Where could we get enough bread in the wilderness to fill such a great multitude?” {Mt} Jesus asked them, “How many loaves do you have?” “Seven,” they said, “and a few little fish.” {Mt}

So He commanded the multitude to sit down on the ground. He took the seven loaves, gave thanks, broke them and gave them to His disciples to set before the people. Then He blessed the few small fish and told the disciples to serve those as well. {Mk}

They all ate and were filled, and the disciples took up seven large baskets of leftover fragments. About four thousand had eaten, {Mk} counting only the men, besides women and children. {Mt} Then Jesus sent the people home.
differences: In Matthew the disciples answer “Seven, and a few little fish”; in Mark they say “Seven,” and the fish are mentioned afterward, when Jesus blesses them separately.
Matthew counts four thousand men “besides women and children”; Mark says “about four thousand.”
Only Mark adds that some in the crowd “have come from afar.”
The disciples’ question differs in wording: “Where could we get enough bread in the wilderness” (Matthew) and “How can one satisfy these people with bread here in the wilderness?” (Mark).

fit.question: This story is very like the feeding of the five thousand. Is it the same event told twice?

points.label: Jesus Himself counts two
points.text: In Mark 8:19–20 Jesus asks the disciples about both meals: five loaves for the five thousand with twelve baskets left over, and seven loaves for the four thousand with seven large baskets. Matthew records the same questions (Matthew 16:9–10).

points.label: Different details throughout
points.text: The crowds, the places, the length of time with Jesus (one day or three), the loaves, the counts and even the Greek word for basket all differ. The first crowd sat on green grass at Passover; this one sat on the ground.

fit.note: Jesus spoke of two feedings, and two Gospels record both; the likeness shows a pattern in His care, not a confusion in the record.
fit.short: Two events. Jesus Himself recalls both feedings, with different loaves, crowds and baskets (Mark 8:19–20).

scene.label: The Decapolis
scene.text: The name means “Ten Cities,” a group of Greek-style towns mostly east of the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee. Many who lived there were Gentiles, though Jews lived in the region too.

scene.label: Three days
scene.text: A crowd in the open country would have carried only a little food. After three days, whatever they brought was gone, and for some the walk home was long.

scene.label: Large baskets
scene.text: At the first feeding the Gospels use a word for a small carrying basket. Here they use a different word, a large hamper, the kind in which Paul was let down over the wall of Damascus “in a large basket” (Acts 9:25).

scene.label: A table in the wilderness
scene.text: Israel once complained, “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Psalm 78:19). The disciples’ question about bread “in the wilderness” sounds much the same. Jesus answers with bread, as God once answered with manna.

witnesses.matthew: Sets the meal right after Jesus heals the lame, the blind, the mute and the maimed on a mountainside, where the crowd “glorified the God of Israel” (Matthew 15:31). As with the five thousand, he counts the men and adds “besides women and children.”
witnesses.mark: Alone notes that some had come “from afar” and that Jesus blessed the fish separately. Mark places this meal just before the scene in the boat where Jesus makes the disciples count the baskets from both feedings (Mark 8:19–20).

seeing.reveals: Jesus notices the crowd’s hunger before anyone mentions it. He has counted their three days with Him and thought about their long walk home, and His compassion reaches into a region where many were not Jews.
seeing.living: Jesus noticed hungry people His disciples had not thought about, and then He used those same disciples to feed them. Ask Him for eyes to see the practical needs of people around you, including those outside your usual circle, and serve what He provides.
seeing.ponder: Whose ordinary, everyday needs has Jesus noticed that you have not yet seen?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus’ compassion notices the hungry, even far from home, and does not send them away empty.
preaching.watch_for: Mark tells two feedings, and Jesus Himself joins them in Mark 8:19–20. Preach this meal with the next scenes in view: soon the disciples will worry about bread in a boat with Jesus sitting beside them.
